procedural_history.originating_court: Family Court of competent jurisdiction (implicitly, as the High Court granted liberty to approach it)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Final judgment and order dated 3rd April 2024 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court of Delhi in Writ Petition (Crl.) No. 416 of 2024.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a writ petition (Crl.) in the High Court of Delhi seeking custody of his minor daughter from his sisters-in-law. The High Court initially ordered the appellant to withdraw his case under the Guardians and Wards Act, interacted with the parties, referred the matter to mediation, and arrived at an interim arrangement for visitation rights based on the mediator's report. Ultimately, the High Court disposed of the writ petition by granting liberty to the parties to approach the family court of competent jurisdiction.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed the High Court's final judgment and order to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and quashed and set aside the impugned judgment and order of the High Court.

directions: The impugned judgment and order of the High Court is quashed and set aside

issue.issue_text: Whether a habeas corpus petition is maintainable in matters concerning the custody of a minor child.

facts: A father, the only surviving natural guardian, sought custody of his minor daughter from his sisters-in-law.
The father had previously filed and then withdrawn a petition for custody under the Guardian and Wards Act, 1890.
Subsequently, he filed a habeas corpus petition under Article 226 of the Constitution seeking the child's custody.
The respondents (sisters-in-law) argued that the habeas corpus petition was not maintainable, especially since the father had withdrawn the earlier petition.
law: The Supreme Court stated that there is no "straight-jacket formula" or "hard and fast rule" regarding the maintainability of a habeas corpus petition in child custody matters.

The court cited its own precedents, including the cases of *Nirmala* and *Tejaswini Gaud*, to establish that the decision to exercise jurisdiction under Article 226 depends on the specific "facts and circumstances of each case."
The court also referenced Section 6 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, which establishes the father as the natural guardian with a legal right to claim custody of his child.
A natural guardian is justified in invoking the "extraordinary remedy" of a habeas corpus writ to seek custody.
application: The Court applied the principle that there is no absolute bar to filing a habeas corpus petition for child custody.
It rejected the respondents' argument that the withdrawal of the previous petition under the 1890 Act prevented the father from filing the current habeas corpus petition.
By referencing the *Tejaswini Gaud* case, which had very similar facts and where a habeas corpus petition was allowed, the Court found the father's petition in the present case to be justified.
The Court emphasized a flexible, case-by-case approach over a rigid procedural rule.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a habeas corpus petition is maintainable in matters concerning the custody of a minor child. It held that there is no absolute rule, and the decision to entertain such a petition must be made based on the specific facts and circumstances of each individual case.

issue.issue_text: What is the paramount consideration in matters of custody of minor children.

law.fact_text: A common thread in all judgments concerning the custody of minor children is the paramount welfare of the child.

application.fact_text: The Court stated that there cannot be any "straight-jacket formula" or "hard and fast rule" in custody matters.
The determination of what is in the child's best welfare must be based on the specific facts and circumstances of each case, and the court cannot take a pedantic approach.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the paramount consideration in matters of custody of minor children is the welfare of the child, which must be determined based on the facts and circumstances of each individual case rather than a rigid formula.

issue.issue_text: Whether the father, as the only natural guardian, should be granted custody of the minor child over relatives who had temporary custody.

facts: The case involves a father, the only surviving biological parent, seeking custody of his minor daughter from his sister-in-laws.
The father's wife passed away just ten days after the daughter's birth, and he also lost his own father to Covid-19.
Due to these tragic circumstances, the father gave temporary custody of his infant daughter to his sister-in-law as a "stop-gap solution."
The father later remarried and, being in a stable position to care for his daughter, sought her custody, which the sister-in-laws refused.
The father is a well-educated Government Official residing in Delhi, while the sister-in-law lives in a remote village.
law: The paramount consideration in all child custody matters is the welfare of the minor child.
Under Section 6 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, the father is the natural guardian of a minor child and has a legal right to claim custody.
A habeas corpus petition under Article 226 of the Constitution is a maintainable remedy in child custody matters, and its applicability depends on the facts and circumstances of each case.
application: The Court established that the sister-in-laws had no legal authority to retain custody, whereas the father, as the natural guardian, had a clear legal right.

It reasoned that the temporary custody granted to the relatives out of necessity does not extinguish the father's right as the natural guardian. The fact that they cared for the child for a few years was not a sufficient ground to deny custody to the father.
The Court determined that the child's welfare would be best served by living with her "natural family," which includes her father and biological brother.
It was noted that the father could provide better educational opportunities and a stable family environment, and that a young child would adapt well to living with her natural family.
The Court concluded that depriving the child of her father's company was not in her best interest.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the father's appeal, concluding that as the only natural guardian, he should be granted custody. This decision was based on both his legal right as a natural guardian and the Court's assessment that living with her natural family was in the paramount welfare of the child. The Court therefore ordered the sister-in-laws to hand over custody to the father.

cases.case_name: Tejaswini Gaud and Others v. Shekhar Jagdish Prasad Tewari and Others
cases.principle: A father, being the natural guardian under Section 6 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, has the legal right to claim custody of his minor child and is justified in invoking the extraordinary remedy of a writ of habeas corpus under Article 226 of the Constitution of India to seek custody.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In matters of child custody, the paramount welfare of the child is the determinative factor. There is no absolute rule regarding the maintainability of a habeas corpus petition for child custody; the court's jurisdiction will be exercised based on the facts and circumstances of each case. The fact that a temporary custodian has cared for a minor child for a period of time is not, by itself, a sufficient ground to deny custody to the child's natural guardian.
obiter: There cannot be any straight-jacket formula.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that custody must be granted to the appellant-father, reasoning that as the only natural guardian, his claim is superior to that of relatives who had temporary custody. The court's decision rests on the principle that the paramount welfare of the child is best served by living with her 'natural family.' The court held that merely because the relatives took care of the child for some time due to unfortunate circumstances, they cannot retain custody, especially when the natural parent has not abandoned the child. The court also found that the child, being of a 'tender age,' would adapt to her natural family in a short period.
legal_tests_applied: In matters of the custody of minor children, the paramount consideration is the welfare of the child, which has to be determined owing to the facts and circumstances of each case without a 'pedantic approach' or 'straight-jacket formula'.

The maintainability of a habeas corpus petition in custody matters is not subject to any 'hard and fast rule' and the court's exercise of jurisdiction depends on the facts and circumstances of each case.
policy_considerations: The court emphasized that in order to ensure the welfare of a minor child, she should live with her 'natural family,' reinforcing the societal value placed on the biological family unit.

The judgment establishes that temporary custody given to relatives during a period of crisis (like the illness of parents) does not extinguish the rights of a natural guardian who has not abandoned the child, preventing temporary arrangements from becoming grounds for permanent separation.
